Fake software updates could pass signature checks, RSA-encrypted data could be read, and systems across the internet would have to migrate off RSA fast.

item.title: @karpathy：Karpathy使用Claude开发结合美国真实公开数据的文明风格游戏地图
item.description:
I asked Claude to populate a Civilization-style game map with real data from the US. Opus 5.5 downloaded and parse a ton of public data and 7 hours and 45K lines of code later... it works :)

- 31 real data sources including Census, BEA, BLS, EIA, NOAA, USGS, DoD, NPS, FAA, FEMA, CDC...
- Real elevation, land cover, GDP, jobs, power plants, mines, ports, airports, bases, parks, universities, freight flows, disasters; all reconciled onto one 25 km hex grid.
- The data is converted into Civilization language, e.g. Gold yield is GDP. A city's districts are its real industry specializations: San Jose gets a Campus, Detroit is "Motor city". Its citizens are its real workforce: 1 in 4 San Jose workers are engineers, coders or scientists, against 1 in 14 nationally. Wonders are chosen by published rules, such as national parks by visitor numbers and universities by R&D spending, etc etc.
- 19 lenses (income, degrees, faith, disasters…), a City View for 524 metros, and nine advisors plus an Explorer. The Explorer turns any column for any of 3,100+ counties into a table and scatter plot, linked to the map.
- Claude decided to skip a few states and territories sry
- Built using Claude Code desktop app, Opus 5.5 on medium and turning on ultracode.

item.title: 【回复】@NickTimiraos：分析回顾前美联储官员凯文·沃什对市场信号与央行货币政策反应的历史观点
item.description:
回复 @NickTimiraos
How would the Warsh Fed address market signals saying financial conditions are tightening, with an inflation picture that still looks uncomfortably hot? I wrote about the issue here: https://www.wsj.com/economy/central-banking/wild-market-swings-are-colliding-with-a-fed-bent-on-taming-inflation-73ccab56?st=sd2tND&reflink=desktopwebshare_permalink  Despite some easy parallels to the December 2018 situation the Powell Fed faced (A new chair! Trump facing a midterm setback! A hawkish committee! Risk-off!), the inflation backdrop is so different that the comparison struggles to reveal much.

Consider: At that December meeting, the committee's leading intellectual dove, Jim Bullard of the St. Louis Fed, warned colleagues that raising rates risked looking "tone deaf." He presciently predicted that the yield curve would invert if they kept going. But he added a caveat that looks very different today: 

"Taking these types of risks at a meeting like this might be worth it if inflation was running above target and we really felt that we had to be aggressive to keep inflation and inflation expectations contained. But it's not running above target."
原帖

回复 @NickTimiraos
Before he became Fed chairman, Kevin Warsh spoke about the value of market signals and the risks of reacting too much to investors' whims. His view, in essence, is that the Fed should treat markets as valuable sources of information, not as something to protect. Watch them closely so as not to be caught flat-footed. But don't let falling prices push it into rescuing investors.

The trouble is that in real time, heeding a market signal and providing a put can look a lot alike. His comments are consistent in principle but hard to apply in practice. In December 2018, at a drawdown much like this month's, he came down on the side of pausing. 

• In a March 2016 speech, he faulted the Fed for "a systematic under-appreciation of contemporaneous market price signals, typically followed by a belated and panicky policy response that validates market assumptions of a central bank put." https://www.hoover.org/research/challenging-groupthink-guild-0

• In October 2018, on Jim Grant's podcast, he presciently noted how rising 10-year Treasury yields (which were up 20 bps that week) would hit risk assets, but he didn't sound concerned: "I'm waiting for some commentator to call this another tantrum with yields moving up so swiftly. I would call it something else. I'd call it nature, gravity." He went on to explain his view that "10-year treasury yields should be equal to nominal GDP."

"The Federal Reserve and other forecasters now appear to have been mugged by the recent data. So real economy's growing at 3.5%. Inflation, at least as measured by the government, is growing at 2%. So history and theory would say 10-year yields should be five and a half or so. So I'm not that overwhelmed by a 20 basis point move this week, but I think nature takes it in that direction."  Whether the Fed raised rates by 25 basis points in December "doesn't matter much in my view. The real job is to think hard about tail risks ... and upside risks."
He referred to the episode in early 2016, when an 11% stock drop led the Fed to defer rate hikes: "We'll need to watch the central bank and see how responsive they are to what I would say natural movements in asset prices… I hope that the focus is on the real side of the real economy rather than worried about what happens if the stock market falls 10% or bond yields move up 50 or 75 basis points. That ought not be their focus." https://podcasts.apple.com/ug/podcast/kevin-warsh-former-federal-reserve-governor/id1207583745?i=1000421382900

• Most memorably, in December 2018, ten weeks later, in a WSJ op-ed with Stan Druckenmiller, with stocks down ~11%: Market indicators "aren't foolproof, but they have a better track record than economists," and the Fed "should cease—for now—its double-barreled blitz of higher interest rates and tighter liquidity." https://www.wsj.com/articles/quantitative-tightening-not-now-11544991760?st=TcJTUZ&reflink=desktopwebshare_permalink

Rex can now resume your programs through a server restart! This is based on a brand new terminal protocol we're also publishing today (OSC 7577) that we worked on in collaboration with @herdrdev with review from multiple terminal emulator and terminal program authors. Link: https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/build/program-resume

This means that ANY program can restart, not just agentic coding tools, and it doesn't require any special integration with any specific terminal or out-of-band protocol. It's plain old terminal escape sequences that are easily implemented by any program!

Rex is shipping with built-in support for Claude Code to start (we emit OSC 7577 in a session start hook), but hope that other programs will adopt this and enable restart.

Program restart in terminals is fundamentally unsafe, so a lot of effort was put into making this as safe as possible. Ultimately, the security of this lies in the terminal emulator.

For Rex, we have a highly flexible Lua-based configuration to opt-in to resume on a program-by-program basis. You can filter by program name, path, working directory, command-line flags, and more. You can also disable the whole thing with one line.

item.title: 【回复】@natolambert：评论指出企业文化可能在无意间形成并对公司发展产生深远影响
item.description:
被回答的问题 @DarioAmodei
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

RoboFinals RL-Env fixes both. Each task starts as a person doing the real work, captured by Lightwheel EgoSuite, and ends as an environment you can train in.

item.title: 【回复】@sayashk：管理咨询不是人工智能的简单包装：探讨人工智能对特定领域影响的文章发布
item.description:
回复 @sayashk
Many discussions of AI’s economic impact assume that knowledge work is a “thin wrapper” on intelligence. In this view, the main job of a knowledge worker is to process information. Once AI can match the quality of expert responses in a domain, it should be able to take over most of the work in that domain.

But actually understanding how an industry creates value paints a very different picture. In a new essay, we conduct this analysis for management consulting.

A summary of our arguments

1. Apocalyptic predictions about consulting misunderstand what clients pay for.

Consulting firms’ provide five different sources of value. Analysis is the most visible, but clients also pay for judgment, coordination, credibility, and accountability. AI has improved dramatically at analysis. But training AI to have judgment has proven harder. As AI capabilities improve, that might change.

But even if AI gets good at judgment, companies still need to persuade competing managers within the firm to agree on recommendations, especially when those recommendations negatively affect them. They need to give key decisions credibility with decision makers such as the board. And they need someone to answer for the results when things go wrong. Consulting firms provide the coordination, credibility, and accountability for all of these.

2. Clients’ AI integration needs are creating demand for consulting.

Past general-purpose technologies, such as business computing and the web, did not just make existing work cheaper. They changed the nature of what clients needed help with, and in the process, they created new work for outside experts, including consultants.

Early evidence shows that AI is doing the same. Realizing the benefits of AI requires organizational transformation, which is increasing the demand for consulting companies. Improvements in AI’s cybersecurity capabilities have also led to organizations taking cyber defense more seriously, and consulting firms are helping them strategize and implement defenses.

3. For consulting firms to capture this demand, they need to change how they operate.

Our analysis in the previous parts does not mean that today’s consulting firms are safe. Clients’ own teams will compete for some of the new demand that we predict will arise due to AI. AI companies are building deployment businesses of their own, even as they sign partnerships with consulting firms.

For consulting firms to successfully adapt to AI, they need to make changes to their operating model: building know-how that clients lack, developing in-house AI expertise and partnering with AI companies on deployment, and staying neutral across model providers.

——

More broadly, one of our goals at @stabl_ai is to deeply understand how institutions can adapt to AI. When discussions of AI's impacts happen in a vacuum, they lead to poor mental models for how AI will impact the work. This essay is the latest in our work on better understanding AI's impacts, and we hope to do a lot more.

at a high level you need:

- "intelligent compute" to run on top of those traces and help you make sense of whats going on

over the past few months we've been working on this "intelligent compute". this has looked like:
- (basic) online evals, jev-as-a-judge, etc

- insights: cluster traces by usage patterns

item.title: @SemiconductorsX：SK海力士计划在4到5年内实现100层3D DRAM量产，预计2031年左右实现商业化
item.description:
SK Hynix targets first 3D DRAM at 100 layers. Mass production is set for 4 to 5 years.

Choi Kang-sik, a distinguished engineer, said on the 25th at the Seoul National University AI Semiconductor Forum that the company is developing 3D DRAM with volume production in mind within that window. Commercialization is expected around 2031. Matching current 10-nm-class density needs about 75 layers. Extra factors push the first product to start at 100 layers.
$SKHY
Current equipment can handle that layer count. 200 to 300 layers and above will need dedicated tools. Longer term, the company is looking at multi-stacking and hybrid bonding used in 3D NAND to reach beyond 1,000 layers. It has already built 3D DRAM cells and verified operation. Refresh characteristics match existing DRAM.

3D DRAM stacks memory cells vertically. It is different from HBM or logic-on-DRAM stacking. The shift comes as planar scaling hits limits. Smaller cells hold less charge and raise leakage and resistance. Stacking upward solves the charge problem and lifts density.

The structure uses layered silicon and silicon-germanium that are etched. Higher layer counts make connections more complex and etching harder. SK Hynix is studying a selector structure that activates only needed circuits to cut area and electrical load. Cost reduction looks at etch process integration from 3D NAND.

It is also researching a switch from silicon to IGZO for the transistor channel. IGZO has lower leakage and can extend data retention. Hydrogen sensitivity remains a challenge. Choi said reliable IGZO could become a game changer for 3D DRAM.

How much of the 100-layer first product stays on current tools once the 4-to-5-year production window starts?
